title: Brown Soda Bread
subtitle: Irish wholemeal loaf raised with bicarbonate of soda
excerpt: Brown soda bread uses bicarbonate of soda and buttermilk to rise, with no yeast and no kneading. It bakes in under an hour and is best eaten on the day, still warm from the oven. Serves 8 to 10 slices.
sourceNotes: Soda bread became the staple bread of Ireland in the 1840s, when bicarbonate of soda became widely available and replaced the yeast-leavened breads that required a starter culture and long proving time. The combination of bicarbonate of soda with acidic buttermilk produces a reliable rise without yeast or kneading. Maura Laverty, Flour Economy (1940s, Irish Food Board archives), and Florence Irwin, The Cookin' Woman: Irish Country Recipes (1949), both document the regional variations: plain white soda bread (farl in Ulster) and the wholemeal brown version standard in the south and west of Ireland. The traditional cross cut into the top is said to let the fairies out; in practice it helps the bread bake evenly to the centre.

recipe.freezeNotes: Slice and freeze. Toast from frozen.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Soda bread is best on the day. Day-old bread is good toasted.

glossaryTerms.definition: A chemical raising agent (baking soda) that reacts with acidic ingredients such as buttermilk to produce carbon dioxide bubbles. It is not the same as baking powder, which contains its own acid.

The slightly sour, acidic liquid left after churning butter, or a cultured dairy product with a similar flavour and acidity. Its acid reacts with bicarbonate of soda to raise the bread. If unavailable, use milk acidified with a tablespoon of lemon juice or white vinegar.

content.text: Brown soda bread is one of the quickest breads there is. It needs no yeast, no kneading, and no proving time. The rise comes from
. Mix the dough, shape it roughly, cut a cross in the top, and it goes straight into the oven. From mixing bowl to table takes about an hour.

The dough should be shaggy and slightly sticky. Do not knead it: overworking activates the gluten and makes the crumb tough. Handle it as little as possible, shape it into a round with wet or floured hands, and get it into the oven quickly before the gas produced by the bicarb dissipates.

content.text: Heat the oven to 200°C fan (220°C conventional). Line a baking tray with baking parchment or dust with flour.

Combine {{wholemeal-flour}} of wholemeal flour, {{plain-flour}} of plain flour, {{bicarbonate-of-soda}} of bicarbonate of soda, and {{salt-table}} of salt in a large bowl. Stir with a fork to mix the raising agent evenly through the flours.

Make a well in the centre and pour in {{buttermilk}} of buttermilk. Mix with a fork or your hand until the dough just comes together. It should be shaggy and tacky, not smooth. Add a little more buttermilk if it seems dry.

Turn the dough onto the prepared tray. Shape it quickly into a round about 20 cm across and 5 cm tall. Do not knead. Scatter oats over the top if using. Use a sharp knife to cut a deep cross into the top of the loaf, going almost all the way through.
Bake for 40 to 45 minutes until the crust is deep brown and the loaf sounds hollow when tapped on the base. Cool on a wire rack for at least 10 minutes before cutting. The crumb sets as it cools.

items.symptom: Centre is raw after the stated time
items.cause: Loaf is too thick, or oven not hot enough
items.fix: Make sure the loaf is no more than 5 cm tall. Test by tapping the base; it should sound hollow. If not, return to the oven directly on the rack for 10 more minutes.

items.symptom: Crust is hard and dark but crumb is dry and dense
items.cause: Too much bicarbonate of soda, or overworked dough
items.fix: Measure the bicarb carefully. Mix only until the dough comes together; any further working develops gluten and tightens the crumb.

items.symptom: Bread has a strong soapy or metallic taste
items.cause: Too much bicarbonate of soda, or bicarb not fully combined
items.fix: The metallic taste comes from undissolved or excess bicarb. Sift it into the flour and measure exactly.

content.text: Soda bread is the everyday bread of rural Ireland. Before ovens became common, it was baked in a cast iron bastible pot over a peat fire, which is why the cross cut is so important: it allowed heat to reach the centre. The brown version, using wholemeal flour, is standard in the south and west of Ireland. In Ulster a white soda bread cut into flat triangles (farls) is more common. Both are eaten with butter, used to mop up stews, or served alongside soup. The ease and speed of the recipe is entirely its point.
